about.title: Thousand Oaks Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Offices, medical facilities, retail centers along Thousand Oaks Boulevard, and construction sites around Ventura County all share one thing: sometimes people get hurt doing their jobs. When that happens in Thousand Oaks, California law usually routes the claim through workers' compensation. Fault does not matter, and in exchange you generally cannot sue your employer directly. That is the basic trade. What many injured workers do not realize is that the story can have a second chapter. If someone other than your employer contributed to the injury, whether a subcontractor on the site, the owner of the property where you were working, the maker of equipment that failed, or another driver who hit you while you were on a work run along US-101 or Moorpark Road, you may have a separate claim against that third party. Those claims sit outside the comp system and carry a two-year filing deadline. We handle both tracks directly and can tell you plainly where you stand.

whyChoose.title: Why Thousand Oaks Workers Choose Us

items.title: Two Claims, Not One
items.desc: Workers' comp is normally your only remedy against your employer, but a negligent subcontractor, property owner, equipment manufacturer, or driver can be held responsible separately. We can evaluate both.

items.title: The 30-Day Report Window Matters
items.desc: California expects you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, and retaliating against you for doing so is illegal. Getting our read early helps you avoid missteps that weaken either claim.

items.title: Contingency, With a Two-Year Clock
items.desc: Third-party injury claims in California must generally be filed within two years, and we work on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery. You lose nothing by asking.

items.question: I was rear-ended on the Ventura Freeway while driving for my employer in Thousand Oaks. Is that workers' comp or a car accident case?
items.answer: It can be both. Because you were working, the injury likely falls under workers' compensation, which pays regardless of who caused the crash. At the same time, the other driver is a third party, so you may also have a separate injury claim against them. Thousand Oaks recorded 616 injury collisions in 2025, and a share of those involve people simply doing their jobs on US-101, Thousand Oaks Boulevard, or Hillcrest Drive.

items.question: Can my employer fire me for filing a workers' comp claim?
items.answer: No. California law makes it illegal for an employer to retaliate against you for reporting a work injury or filing a claim. If you have been demoted, cut back, or let go after reporting, tell us, because that conduct can create its own claim.

items.question: What if I missed the 30-day reporting deadline?
items.answer: Report it now anyway, in writing, and note why the delay happened. A late report can complicate a comp claim, but it does not necessarily end it, and it has no bearing on a third-party claim, which follows the two-year deadline instead. We can sort out which rules apply to your situation.
